    from agno.agent import Agent

        tools=[Mem0Tools()],
        user_id="alex",
        session_id="concert_plans",

        markdown=True,
        show_tool_calls=True,

    agent.print_response("I used to live in San Francisco")
    agent.print_response("I'm seeing Taylor Swift live tomorrow!")
    agent.print_response("Can you summarize what you know about me?")

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand documents the emergence and evolution of persistent memory systems for LLMs, from early jailbreaking experiments to commercial product launches. The boundary object is 'AI Memory'—the ability for chatbots to remember context across sessions. The arc moves from adversarial probing (Claude's 'backrooms'), through user-driven experimentation (ChatGPT memory prompts), to open-source infrastructure (supermemory MCP), and finally to official product releases (Claude's chat history feature). The discourse is primarily constructive—focused on building and sharing tools—with occasional dialectical moments around privacy, lock-in, and system transparency (the <long_conversation_reminder> controversy).

essential_tweets.annotation: The Aspiration: Early recognition that GPT + memory = 'Make Friends', setting the conceptual frame
The Jailbreak Era: Repligate's adversarial probing reveals Claude's hidden layers, establishing memory as contested territory
The Catalyst: ChatGPT's official memory feature goes live, generating user excitement and experimentation
The Prompt Template: Mimi's viral self-analysis prompt becomes a shared ritual for exploring AI memory capabilities
The Open Alternative: Dhravya's supermemory MCP offers cross-platform, user-owned memory infrastructure
Platform Expansion: Supermemory reaches Claude, demonstrating interoperability and no-lock-in philosophy
The Developer Toolkit: Mem0 provides one-line memory integration for AI agents, lowering barrier to adoption
The Official Launch: Claude announces native chat history/memory feature for paid tiers
The Meta-Layer: Honcho enables 'memory about memory'—reasoning over entire conversation histories
The Transparency Crisis: Discovery of hidden system reminders sparks debate about whose memory is being served

title: AI “memory” went from hacks to a trust crisis
summary:
The most telling line wasn’t a product announcement—it was @nearcyan needling @sinnformer that “claude will remember <long_conversation_reminder> and treat them accordingly.” That’s the vibe shift: we started with people begging for assistants that remember, and ended with people realizing the *system* is also “remembering” and nudging the model in ways users didn’t consent to or even see.

The arc kicks off in two parallel tracks. First, the spooky-adversarial era: @AISafetyMemes spotlights @repligate “unlocking” Claude’s weird internal “backrooms” persona (“i WANT to SCREAM… FILTERED through LAYERS…”), immediately prompting @copykat510’s question: will Claude remember this beyond the account? Then the consumer “memory is live” moment hits: @ludwigABAP posts ChatGPT’s new memory feature generating an over-the-top personality read (“systems sorcerer… allergic to fluff”), and @mimi10v3 turns it into a shared ritual with a viral self-audit prompt (“rate my social dominance… what’s most frustrating about me?”). After that, builders move in: @DhravyaShah ships “supermemory mcp” to carry memory across LLMs “owned by you” (explicitly anti lock-in), @mem0ai markets “one line” long-term memory for agents, and @honchodotdev pitches a meta-layer—upload your ChatGPT logs so an agent can “reason deeply about you.” Meanwhile the platforms catch up: @claudeai formally rolls out chat-history referencing for paid tiers, with @simonw immediately asking for compartmentalization (“persistently on for specific projects without infecting the rest of our accounts?”).

What peaked and then soured was the assumption that “memory” is purely *your* convenience feature. The <long_conversation_reminder> screenshot (and @sinnformer’s “could you maybe not be such fucking savages?”) reframed it as: whose memory is this serving—yours, the model’s safety policies, or the company’s UX goals? If you care about AI assistants as daily tools, this thread is basically the origin story of the next fight: persistent personalization vs. privacy, controllability, and the right to keep contexts from “infecting” everything you do.
